question: Which US retail brokerage channels were identified for IPO share sales, and which investors were eligible for the European retail tranche?
answer:
Based on the IPO filings, the U.S. retail brokerage channels and the eligible investors for the European retail tranche are identified as follows:

### U.S. Retail Brokerage Channels
The U.S. preliminary prospectus identifies the following broker-dealers and online brokerage platforms acting as selling group members through which retail investors could be offered shares:
* Charles Schwab & Co., Inc. [US-PROSPECTUS | UNDERWRITING > Sales to Retail Investors | p. 339]
* Fidelity Brokerage Services LLC and Fidelity Capital Markets (a division of National Financial Services LLC) [US-PROSPECTUS | UNDERWRITING > Sales to Retail Investors | p. 339]
* Robinhood Financial, LLC [US-PROSPECTUS | UNDERWRITING > Sales to Retail Investors | p. 339]
* Trade-PMR, Inc. [US-PROSPECTUS | UNDERWRITING > Sales to Retail Investors | p. 339]
* SoFi Securities LLC [US-PROSPECTUS | UNDERWRITING > Sales to Retail Investors | p. 339]
* E*TRADE from Morgan Stanley (an affiliate of one of the representatives of the underwriters) [US-PROSPECTUS | UNDERWRITING > Sales to Retail Investors | p. 339]

### Eligible Investors for the European Retail Tranche
The European retail offering is solely addressed to:
1. **Retail Investors in Covered EEA Countries:** Individual persons or legal entities that do not qualify as "qualified investors" within the meaning of Article 2 point (e) of the Prospectus Regulation, and that are resident or located in one of the Covered EEA Countries (Germany, Denmark, Finland, France, Ireland, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, and Sweden) [EU-PROSPECTUS | 8. Details of the Offer > 8.1 Terms and Conditions of the Offer > 8.1.1 Eligible Retail Investors | p. 202, EU-PROSPECTUS | Summary of the Prospectus > D. Key Information on the Offer of Securities to the Public and Admission to Trading on a Regulated Market > D.1 Under which conditions and timetable can I invest in this security? | p. S-5].
2. **Financial Intermediaries:** Financial intermediaries acting on behalf of retail investors, or acting as a fiduciary or agent for one or more investor accounts, provided that each such account is a retail investor and the financial intermediary has investment discretion with respect to each such account [EU-PROSPECTUS | 8. Details of the Offer > 8.1 Terms and Conditions of the Offer > 8.1.1 Eligible Retail Investors | p. 202].

question: For which purposes did Anthropic state it intended to use the net proceeds from the offering and the concurrent private placement, including the specified RSU tax-withholding obligation?
answer:
Based on the preliminary prospectus, Anthropic stated that it intends to use the net proceeds from the offering and the concurrent private placement for the following purposes:

* **General corporate purposes:** Including working capital, operating expenses, and capital expenditures (such as investments in compute and infrastructure), as well as the hiring and retention of highly skilled personnel [US-PROSPECTUS | USE OF PROCEEDS | p. 128].
* **Acquisitions and investments:** A portion of the net proceeds may be used to acquire or invest in businesses, products, services, or technologies (though there were no agreements or commitments for any material acquisitions or investments at that time) [US-PROSPECTUS | USE OF PROCEEDS | p. 128].
* **RSU Settlement tax obligations:** A portion of the net proceeds will be used to satisfy anticipated tax withholding and remittance obligations of $3.8 billion related to the RSU Settlement [US-PROSPECTUS | USE OF PROCEEDS | p. 128]. This figure is based on an assumed initial public offering price of $74.00 per share (the midpoint of the estimated price range) and an assumed tax withholding rate of 50.90%, with each $1.00 increase or decrease in the assumed IPO price changing the required obligation by $52 million [US-PROSPECTUS | USE OF PROCEEDS | p. 128].

Anthropic noted that it will have broad discretion in using these proceeds and cannot further specify particular uses with certainty [US-PROSPECTUS | USE OF PROCEEDS | p. 128].

question: What director appointment and removal rights did the Long-Term Benefit Trust generally hold through Class T common stock?
answer:
Through Class T common stock, the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT) generally holds the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together constitute a majority of the authorized members of the board of directors [US-PROSPECTUS | OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS > Long-Term Benefit Trust > Election and Removal of Directors | p. 253]. 

The specifics and limitations regarding these rights include:
* **Exclusion from Other Classes:** Class T common stock does not vote on the election or removal of directors elected by holders of Class A and Class F common stock, which are elected or removed solely by holders of Class A and Class F common stock voting together [US-PROSPECTUS | OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS > Long-Term Benefit Trust > Election and Removal of Directors | p. 253].
* **Notice Requirement:** Prior to nominating or removing a director, the nominating party must provide at least 30 days’ notice to the Nominating and Governance Committee (NGC), which notice period can be waived by the NGC in its discretion [US-PROSPECTUS | OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS > Long-Term Benefit Trust > Election and Removal of Directors | p. 253].
* **Specified Class T Director Limitations:** For one specific director seat (the "Specified Class T Director"), the LTBT's ability to nominate, remove without cause, or change the designation is subject to the concurrence of the NGC. If the NGC does not concur within 15 days, the matter is submitted to a vote of Class E common stock (requiring a majority of votes cast, subject to a quorum of a majority of outstanding Class E common stock), unless the LTBT withdraws the notice [US-PROSPECTUS | OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS > Long-Term Benefit Trust > Election and Removal of Directors | p. 253].
* **Removal for Cause:** Any Class T director (including the Specified Class T Director) may be removed for cause under Delaware law without NGC concurrence or Class E approval, provided that both the LTBT and Founder LLC give 30 calendar days' notice to each other and the NGC prior to effecting such removal [US-PROSPECTUS | OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS > Long-Term Benefit Trust > Election and Removal of Directors | p. 253].

Our concentration in a limited number of products and applications, as well as our focused development strategy within specific areas of the broader AI landscape, reduces our ability to mitigate business risks through diversification. Many of our competitors offer diverse product portfolios across multiple business lines or pursue broader development across AI modalities, enabling them to offset weaknesses in a particular area. In contrast, any decline in demand for our core offerings, whether due to competition, technological changes, pricing pressure, changes in customer demand, or other factors, would have a direct and disproportionate impact on our revenue and ability to achieve and sustain profitability. Our concentration also reflects a strategy that prioritizes model capability as a principal source of differentiation and relies substantially on organic adoption rather than a large direct sales organization. question: For whom was Class E common stock intended, and what voting and economic rights did that class have?
answer:
* **Intended Recipients:** Class E common stock is intended to be issued to employees, excluding co-founders, as follows: (i) one share of Class E common stock for each six months of employment completed with the company, and (ii) one share of Class E common stock for each share of Class A common stock that such employee has pledged to donate through the donation matching program or any similar program established in the future [US-PROSPECTUS | OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS > Class E Common Stock | p. 258-259]. 
* **Economic Rights:** 
  * Holders of Class E common stock are not entitled to receive dividends [CHARTER | Article V > Section 5.3 Rights of Class E Common Stock | p. 9-10, US-PROSPECTUS | DESCRIPTION OF CAPITAL STOCK > General | p. 304, EU-PROSPECTUS | Summary of the Prospectus > C. Key Information on the Securities > C.1 What are the main features of the securities? | p. S-5].
  * In the event of liquidation, dissolution, or winding-up, holders of Class E common stock are entitled to receive par value per share but do not otherwise participate in liquidation distributions [US-PROSPECTUS | DESCRIPTION OF CAPITAL STOCK > General | p. 304, EU-PROSPECTUS | Summary of the Prospectus > C. Key Information on the Securities > C.1 What are the main features of the securities? | p. S-5].
  * Class E shares are not transferable and are subject to automatic redemption by the company for no consideration upon the occurrence of certain events (such as the Class F sunset time, death or incapacity, cessation of service for cause, commencement of service with a direct competitor, or separation from employment other than for cause) [CHARTER | Article V > Section 5.3 Rights of Class E Common Stock | p. 9-10, US-PROSPECTUS | OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS > Class E Common Stock | p. 258-259, US-PROSPECTUS | DESCRIPTION OF CAPITAL STOCK > General | p. 304].
* **Voting Rights:** Class E common stock has no right to vote except on certain specified matters (or as otherwise required by law):
  * The nomination or proposed removal of the Specified Class T Director or a change in the director designated as the Specified Class T Director (in circumstances where the Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee does not concur with the Long-Term Benefit Trust’s proposed action) [US-PROSPECTUS | OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS > Class E Common Stock | p. 258-259, US-PROSPECTUS | DESCRIPTION OF CAPITAL STOCK > Common Stock > Voting Rights | p. 305].
  * Certain proposals to amend the terms of the Long-Term Benefit Trust (LTBT) and the rights of Class T common stock, or to redeem Class T common stock [US-PROSPECTUS | OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS > Class E Common Stock | p. 258-259, US-PROSPECTUS | DESCRIPTION OF CAPITAL STOCK > Common Stock > Voting Rights | p. 305].
  * Certain amendments to the amended and restated certificate of incorporation that would adversely affect the powers, preferences, or special rights of Class E common stock, on which the DGCL entitles such holders to vote separately as a class [US-PROSPECTUS | DESCRIPTION OF CAPITAL STOCK > Common Stock > Voting Rights | p. 305].

question: What constituted a quorum of Anthropic’s board under Section 8.7 of the charter?
answer:
Under Section 8.7 of Anthropic's charter, a quorum of the board was constituted as follows:

* **General Rule:** At all meetings of the Board, a majority of the Whole Board, including at least one At-Large Director, constitutes a quorum for the transaction of business [CHARTER | Article VIII > Section 8.7 Board Quorum | p. 20].
* **Second Called Meeting Exception:** If a quorum is not present at a first called meeting solely due to the absence of at least one At-Large Director, the meeting may be reconvened no earlier than 48 hours later (with at least 24 hours' notice given to absent directors). At such a reconvened meeting, a quorum is deemed present if a majority of the Whole Board is present, regardless of whether any At-Large Director is present [CHARTER | Article VIII > Section 8.7 Board Quorum | p. 20].
* **Adjournments:** If a quorum is not present at any meeting, the directors present may adjourn the meeting from time to time without notice other than an announcement at the meeting, subject to the specific restriction that a meeting lacking a quorum solely due to the absence of an At-Large Director may only be adjourned or reconvened in accordance with the 48-hour reconvened meeting rule [CHARTER | Article VIII > Section 8.7 Board Quorum | p. 20].
* **Waiver:** The required attendance of an At-Large Director to establish a quorum may be waived by a majority of the At-Large Directors then in office prior to the meeting [CHARTER | Article VIII > Section 8.7 Board Quorum | p. 20].

question: At the assumed $74.00 price, what were the estimated net proceeds from the offering and the concurrent private placement, and what were the reported total contractual obligations and the type of expense accounting for most of them?
answer:
Based on the preliminary prospectus:

* **Estimated Net Proceeds:** At the assumed initial public offering price of $74.00 per share (the midpoint of the estimated range), the estimated net proceeds from the offering of Class A common stock and the concurrent private placement of Class N common stock are approximately **$84.6 billion** (after deducting estimated underwriting discounts, commissions, and offering expenses, but before any exercise of the underwriters' option to purchase additional shares) [US-PROSPECTUS | USE OF PROCEEDS | p. 128].
* **Total Contractual Obligations:** Total reported contractual obligations as of September 30, 2026, were **$319,993 million** (or approximately **$320.0 billion**) [US-PROSPECTUS | MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Liquidity and Capital Resources > Contractual Obligations | p. 179]. (Additionally, when including short-term commitments, subsequent commitments, and uncommenced leases, aggregate commitments were approximately $900.9 billion) [US-PROSPECTUS | MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Liquidity and Capital Resources > Contractual Obligations | p. 178-179].
* **Type of Expense Accounting for Most of Them:** **Purchase commitments**—primarily consisting of future minimum payments under cloud service provider (CSP) hosting and other third-party infrastructure service agreements related to compute and infrastructure—account for the vast majority of these contractual obligations ($313,819 million out of the $319,993 million total) [US-PROSPECTUS | MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Liquidity and Capital Resources > Contractual Obligations | p. 179], with substantially all of the broader $900.9 billion aggregate commitments also related to **compute and infrastructure** [US-PROSPECTUS | MANAGEMENT’S DISCUSSION AND ANALYSIS OF FINANCIAL CONDITION AND RESULTS OF OPERATIONS > Liquidity and Capital Resources > Contractual Obligations | p. 178-179].

question: Which chip platforms did Anthropic describe in its multi-chip compute strategy, and what separate risk did it disclose about relying on cloud service providers?
answer:
Anthropic disclosed that it relies on a limited number of cloud service providers (CSPs)—specifically Amazon, Google, and Microsoft—and detailed several risks and complex dynamics regarding this reliance:
* **Service Outages and Operational Disruption:** CSPs may experience service outages, security incidents, or capacity constraints that affect operations, and any significant disruption or limitation of access to the infrastructure provided by Amazon, Google, and Microsoft would negatively impact operations and degrade the availability and performance of Anthropic's models, platform, and applications [US-PROSPECTUS | RISK FACTORS > Risks Related to our Business and Industry > Our reliance on a limited number of CSPs and suppliers, some of which have strategic and investment… | p. 77]; [US-PROSPECTUS | RISK FACTORS > Risks Related to our Business and Industry > If we fail to manage our technical operations infrastructure, or experience service outages, interruptions,… | p. 86].
* **Renewal and Transition Challenges:** Contract terms such as pricing, compute commitments, and service levels are subject to negotiation upon renewal, and migrating workloads or transitioning services to alternative providers would be costly, time-consuming, operationally complex, and could degrade compute efficiency and cause operational delays [US-PROSPECTUS | RISK FACTORS > Risks Related to our Business and Industry > Our reliance on a limited number of CSPs and suppliers, some of which have strategic and investment… | p. 77]; [US-PROSPECTUS | RISK FACTORS > Risks Related to our Business and Industry > If we fail to manage our technical operations infrastructure, or experience service outages, interruptions,… | p. 86].
* **Conflicts of Interest and Competing Interests:** Because Amazon, Google, and Microsoft simultaneously serve as investors, customers, distribution partners, and competitors with substantial in-house AI programs, potential conflicts of interest arise where these CSPs may prioritize their own compute needs or those of other competitors, give them visibility into pricing and commercial terms, or promote competing offerings on more favorable terms [US-PROSPECTUS | RISK FACTORS > Risks Related to our Business and Industry > Our reliance on a limited number of CSPs and suppliers, some of which have strategic and investment… | p. 78].
* **Compute Allocation Dependencies:** Anthropic's ability to secure compute is subject to allocation decisions and operational execution by CSPs, meaning Anthropic may not receive the full amount of compute sought or required on necessary timelines due to internal demand or capacity constraints at the providers [US-PROSPECTUS | RISK FACTORS > Risks Related to our Business and Industry > If we are unable to secure adequate compute or if we fail to direct our compute effectively across our… | p. 37].
* **Antitrust Scrutiny:** Relationships with these strategic partners—including exclusive or preferential arrangements, investment ties, bundling of services, or cooperative initiatives—have attracted and may attract antitrust or competition law scrutiny [US-PROSPECTUS | RISK FACTORS > Risks Related to our Business and Industry > Our reliance on a limited number of CSPs and suppliers, some of which have strategic and investment… | p. 78].

[1] [US-PROSPECTUS | BUSINESS > Our Infrastructure > Multi-Chip Compute Approach | p. 213-214]  (preliminary, filed 2026-11-17; chunk US-PROSPECTUS-837461ff51c3291e)
Multi-Chip Compute Approach
We have built a deliberate and diversified compute sourcing strategy across multiple chip platforms that provides the following distinct advantages:
•We can secure compute from multiple providers rather than being constrained by any single provider.
•We can select chips based on the best price-performance and efficiency characteristics for each workload, benefiting from the differentiated strengths of each platform.
•We maintain collaborative relationships with each of our providers, and we influence roadmaps and features of future chip generations. Our chip platforms include:
◦AWS Trainium. Our strategic collaboration with Amazon provides us with access to accelerators, including custom-designed Trainium chips, and compute infrastructure, as well as the opportunity to influence future generations of Trainium chips.
◦Google TPUs. Our partnerships with Google and Broadcom provide us with access to compute capacity powered by Google TPUs across multiple generations of the TPU platform.
◦NVIDIA GPUs. Our strategic partnership with NVIDIA, together with our arrangements with Microsoft, SpaceXAI, Nscale, Lambda, and other cloud providers, provides us with access to compute capacity powered by NVIDIA GPUs, including NVIDIA Grace Blackwell and Vera Rubin GPU systems, as well as the opportunity to collaborate directly with NVIDIA on design and engineering to optimize future NVIDIA hardware for our workload profile.
◦AMD GPUs. Our relationship with AMD, together with our arrangements with approved manufacturers of AMD-based Helios rack-scale systems and third-party service providers, provides us with access to compute capacity powered by AMD Instinct™ GPUs, including AMD Instinct™ MI450 Series GPUs, as well as the opportunity to collaborate directly with AMD through a multi-year engineering collaboration.
•We can onboard new chip platforms in a fraction of the time it once took. Historically, bringing a new chip platform into production required intense engineering effort over many months. By leveraging Claude, our engineering teams can now bring new chip platforms into production more quickly. This speed and efficiency also rely on the robust foundation we have already built across multiple chip families, including a proprietary orchestration layer designed to seamlessly test and measure performance against our actual workloads. As a result, we are able to adopt new accelerators as they become available, expanding our access to compute capacity while reducing our dependence on any single hardware provider.
See the section titled “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations —Liquidity and Capital Resources—Contractual Obligations—Infrastructure Service Arrangements” for more information regarding the terms of these arrangements.

[2] [US-PROSPECTUS | BUSINESS > Our Core Advantages > Our Approach to Compute | p. 197]  (preliminary, filed 2026-11-17; chunk US-PROSPECTUS-a8bf0dff9dfd7b5e)
Our Approach to Compute
Our approach to compute starts with training models that are designed to be more capable and run more efficiently on any given type of compute.
Our ability to build more capable models and serve them more efficiently reflects the compounding returns of an iterative cycle between our pre-training, post-training, and inference research, all of which is enabled by our fungible compute pool. Pre- and post-training research produces proprietary compute multipliers that make our models more capable. Research and inference engineering drive sustained reductions in the compute required to serve those models.
In addition to enabling more capable and efficient models, our multi-chip compute architecture across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs allows us to orchestrate workloads to optimize for price and performance. We have years of experience effectively training and running our models across multiple chip families, which we believe is differentiated and difficult to replicate. This foundation, paired with Claude’s increasing understanding of chip and model architectures, allows us to onboard new chip platforms in a fraction of the time this once required.
Our compute pool is fungible by design. We have made substantial engineering investments to build the internal orchestration, scheduling, and capacity management systems that allow accelerator capacity, regardless of provider, chip architecture, or physical location, to be directed across workloads. The same infrastructure that serves customer workloads is also directed to research, model development, and internal usage of Claude. These systems manage the underlying hardware as a unified capacity pool, monitor utilization and demand across that pool, and direct compute to wherever it is expected to be most productive at any given time.
Our multi-chip compute approach provides us with substantially greater chip access than relying on one platform and enables us to opportunistically capture the price-performance benefits of each chip family and generation. Securing this access requires significant advance commitment. Given the long lead times between contracting for compute and that compute becoming available to serve workloads, we secure compute well in advance of anticipated demand. In some cases, we may also make payments in advance of the delivery of the equipment or infrastructure. We anticipate making significant investments for the foreseeable future, including in compute and infrastructure, to ensure we have the technological resources to maintain and expand our position at the frontier of AI.

Our Approach to Compute. We manage compute as a single, fungible pool from multiple strategic partners, and we dynamically direct available compute between workloads based on where the marginal unit is expected to be most productive at any given time. We believe that this approach to compute enables us to deliver superior models, serve more customers, and achieve greater productivity from our compute investment. This compute efficiency creates the foundation for us to advance frontier capabilities through research and model development, meet growing demand from customers, and provide for internal usage of Claude. We have achieved this through our research breakthroughs and our multi-chip compute architecture across AWS Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs, enabling us to orchestrate workloads to optimize for price and performance. To support our research, model development, customer demand, and internal usage of Claude, we continue to invest at scale. These commitments include approximately $451.6 billion expected to be incurred before December 31, 2030, and substantially all of the remainder is expected to be incurred between 2031 and 2045. Approximately $70.7 billion of these commitments are due in the 12 months following September 30, 2026. Revolving Credit Agreement
In May 2025, we entered into a Credit Agreement (as amended from time to time prior to the A&R Credit Agreement (as defined below), the “Credit Agreement”) with certain lenders from time to time party thereto and Morgan Stanley Senior Funding, Inc., as administrative agent and collateral agent for the lenders, which initially provided for a $2.5 billion senior secured revolving credit facility with a $400 million letter of credit sublimit (the “Initial Credit Facility”). In September 2025, we amended the Initial Credit Facility to increase the aggregate revolving commitments to $2.75 billion, and in November 2025, we further amended the Initial Credit Facility to increase the aggregate revolving commitments to $3.25 billion.
In September 2026, we entered into an Amended and Restated Credit Agreement (the “A&R Credit Agreement”), which amended and restated the Credit Agreement to provide for a $15.0 billion senior secured revolving credit facility with the full amount thereof available for letters of credit (the “A&R Credit Facility”). The A&R Credit Facility will mature on September 4, 2031, subject to earlier springing maturity if more than $500 million in aggregate scheduled cash principal payments on certain of our indebtedness are required within the 91-day period preceding the date on which any such scheduled principal payment is due, and we do not have sufficient liquidity to make all such payments then due and remain in pro forma compliance with our financial covenant, subject to certain other exceptions and conditions set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement. The proceeds of the A&R Credit Facility may be used for working capital, general corporate purposes, and other lawful purposes. We may request borrowings in U.S. dollars or certain other agreed currencies, subject to the terms of the A&R Credit Agreement. As of September 30, 2026, we had no borrowings drawn under the A&R Credit Facility and $205 million of standby letters of credit outstanding. As of September 30, 2026, we were in compliance with all covenants under the A&R Credit Agreement.

From and after the Guarantee and Collateral Release Date, such applicable margin will vary depending on our credit ratings, as more fully set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement. In addition, the A&R Credit Agreement includes customary affirmative and negative covenants, including, but not limited to, restrictions on additional indebtedness, liens, asset sales, investments, mergers, and restricted payments. On and after the Guarantee and Collateral Release Date, the negative covenants limiting asset sales, investments, restricted payments, and affiliate transactions will cease to apply and the negative covenants restricting additional indebtedness and liens will be modified in certain respects, including to permit additional indebtedness, subject to a cap on certain indebtedness that is secured by assets that do not secure the A&R Credit Facility or that is incurred or guaranteed by restricted subsidiaries that are not guarantors under the A&R Credit Facility. question: What IPO lock-up milestone applied to Anthropic’s co-founders, and what distinct conditions could trigger the Class F voting-power sunset?
answer:
Based on the preliminary prospectus, the IPO lock-up terms and conditions triggering the Class F voting-power sunset are as follows:

### **Co-Founder IPO Lock-Up Restrictions**
Our co-founders have agreed with the underwriters that all lock-up securities owned by them (other than Class A shares sold in the offering pursuant to the underwriting agreement) are restricted until the earlier to occur of:
1. 6:00 AM Eastern Time on the second full trading day immediately following the **Q3 Earnings Release Date**; or
2. Immediately after the close of the trading day on the **365th day** after the date of the prospectus [US-PROSPECTUS | UNDERWRITING > Lock-Up and Market Standoff Agreements | p. 337].

Notwithstanding the above, each founder and their signatories may **Transfer up to 29%** of the aggregate number of their lock-up securities (held as of the last day of the month preceding the month of the prospectus date) beginning upon the earlier to occur of:
1. 6:00 AM Eastern Time on the second full trading day immediately following the **Q1 Earnings Release Date**; or
2. Immediately after the close of the trading day on the **180th Day** after the date of the prospectus [US-PROSPECTUS | UNDERWRITING > Lock-Up and Market Standoff Agreements | p. 337].

---

### **Conditions Triggering the Class F Voting-Power Sunset**
The **Class F Sunset Time** occurs on the earlier of:
1. The time when **no Class F common stock remains outstanding**, including due to the redemption of Class F common stock agreed to by a Supermajority of the Continuing Founders or upon the dissolution of the Founder LLC; and
2. The completion of the **Class F Transition Period** [US-PROSPECTUS | OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS > Sunset Provisions | p. 260].

The Class F Transition Period commences when there have been **fewer than three Continuing Founders** (excluding successor members who are "Non-Qualifying Members") for **90 consecutive calendar days** [US-PROSPECTUS | OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS > Sunset Provisions | p. 260]. A Continuing Founder is removed from the Founder LLC upon the earliest to occur of:
* Such Continuing Founder’s resignation as a member of the Founder LLC [US-PROSPECTUS | OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS > Sunset Provisions | p. 260];
* Such Continuing Founder’s death or incapacity [US-PROSPECTUS | OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS > Sunset Provisions | p. 260];
* With respect to each of the seven original co-founders, such original co-founder ceasing to hold (together with related holders) on any record date a number of shares of Class A common stock (including options, RSUs, and other convertible securities) equal to **at least 2%** of the shares of Class A common stock held by them as of the completion of the offering [US-PROSPECTUS | OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS > Sunset Provisions | p. 260];
* Removal for "cause," which includes specified competitive activities described in the Founder LLC Agreement [US-PROSPECTUS | OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS > Sunset Provisions | p. 260];
* With respect to any successor member admitted prior to the transition period (other than a successor member during the transition period), the **tenth anniversary of the completion of this offering** [US-PROSPECTUS | OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS > Sunset Provisions | p. 260]; or
* The commencement of a leave of absence approved by a Supermajority of the other Continuing Founders, subject to certain limitations [US-PROSPECTUS | OUR GOVERNANCE STRUCTURE AND ITS GOALS > Sunset Provisions | p. 260].

Stock-Based Compensation
We measure compensation expense for all stock-based payment awards, including stock options and RSUs, granted to employees, directors, and other service providers, based on the estimated fair value of the awards on the date of grant. The most significant input in determining the fair value of a stock option is the estimated fair value of our common stock. The estimated fair value of our common stock is also used to measure the grant-date fair value of RSUs and RSAs, including those subject to performance-based vesting conditions.
Stock Options
We estimate the fair value of stock options granted to employees, consultants, officers, and directors using the Black-Scholes-Merton option pricing model on the date of grant. The fair value of stock options that are expected to vest is recognized as compensation expense on a straight-line basis over the requisite service period. Forfeitures are accounted for when they occur.
The Black-Scholes-Merton model considers several variables and assumptions in estimating the fair value of stock-based awards. These variables include:
•Fair Value of Common Stock. Because our common stock is not yet publicly traded, we must estimate the fair value of our common stock. Our board of directors considers numerous objective and subjective factors to determine the fair value of our common stock as discussed in the section titled “— Common Stock Valuations” below.
•Expected Volatility. Since we have no trading history of our common stock, the expected volatility of our underlying common stock is estimated by taking the weighted-average historical volatility of a group of comparable publicly traded companies over a period equal to the expected life of the options.
•Expected Term. Expected term represents the period over which we anticipate stock-based awards to be outstanding. We estimate the expected term based on the options’ vesting term and contractual terms, such that the expected life is equal to the average of the stock-based award’s weighted-average vesting period and its contractual term.
•Risk-Free Rate. The expected risk-free rate assumption is based on the U.S. Treasury instruments whose term is consistent with the expected term of the stock options.
•Expected Dividend Yield. The expected dividend yield is zero, as we have never declared or paid any dividends and have no current plans to do so.

Organizations around the world rely on Claude. We serve a breadth of customers, from the largest enterprises to AI-native companies, government and research institutions, as well as prosumers.
As of September 30, 2026, our customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis included every company in the Fortune 10, over 50% of the Fortune 500, and over 30% of the Global 2000. Across industries, enterprises deploy Claude in mission-critical production workflows—for example, underwriting insurance policies, writing clinical reports for life-saving drugs, detecting and remediating cybersecurity threats, and analyzing portfolios for asset managers. Claude has achieved particularly deep adoption in highly regulated sectors where the cost of unreliable AI is prohibitive and trust cannot be retrofitted.
In addition, leading AI-native companies build next-generation coding tools, design platforms, and productivity applications on Claude. Government and research institutions also apply Claude to work that ranges from materials science to energy security; mission-driven organizations use Claude to compress the expected timeline of scientific research, clinical workflows, and the delivery of public benefits.
Our customer base has grown rapidly in both the number and scale of customer relationships, with organizations expanding from initial use cases into enterprise-wide production deployments. As of September 30, 2026, we had more than 11,900 customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis, up from more than 950 as of September 30, 2025.
Our customers fall into two primary categories: enterprises and prosumers.

Our customers’ journey using Claude often begins with a single use case before expanding across departments, applications, and workflows. As our models become more capable, customers often deepen our partnerships— they find more ways to embed Claude into their workflows, increasing the scope of what Claude can accomplish within their enterprises. This pattern of initial deployment, demonstrated value, and rapid expansion has been replicated across organizations and is reflected in our Net Revenue Retention of approximately 900% as of September 30, 2026.
We see this expansion as customers adopt agentic products like Claude Code. For example, in the three months ended September 30, 2026, Claude Enterprise users who did not use Claude Code spent less than $75 per month on average, while the top 5% of Claude Enterprise users who used Claude Code spent approximately 20 times that amount.

The speed and depth of our enterprise customer adoption are powerful evidence of Claude’s position at the frontier of super intelligence. Our customer base as of September 30, 2026 includes:
•More than 11,900 customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis;
•More than 1,900 customers with $1 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis; and
•Approximately 250 customers with $10 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis.
We believe customers choose Claude for a wide variety of use cases, from routine knowledge work to their most important problems. They come to us for access to frontier intelligence across our platform and applications that deliver real-world outcomes. We see this conviction in customer behavior: enterprises consistently utilize our latest and most capable models as soon as they are released, gravitating to the most advanced option for their highest-value work. Our customers see us as a long-term partner for the frontier capabilities we offer today, for the innovation they expect from us in the future, and for our ability to meet their needs across the capability-cost-speed curve.

Despite this growth, our penetration into the largest enterprises remains early. Over 50% of the Fortune 500 and over 30% of the Global 2000 were customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis as of September 30, 2026. We believe we are in the early stages of our expansion within these customers, with our revenue from these Fortune 500 customers representing, on average, less than 0.1% of their total expenses for the three months ended September 30, 2026.
